title: Semiconductor & Silicon Functional Safety
subtitle: RTL × Verification × Lockstep & Redundancy × Hardware Metrics × Certification Leadership
description: A rigorous learning route for functional safety at the semiconductor and silicon IP level, from element-level foundations and digital design through RTL verification, fault injection, lockstep and redundant architectures, hardware safety metrics, Safety Element out of Context authoring, the wider standards landscape and certification-ready technical leadership.
methodTitle: Learn the silicon layer, verify the safety mechanism, then defend the metric and the safety case
methodSteps: Study the stage concept and identify the semiconductor-specific inputs, activities and evidence it produces.
Answer foundation questions precisely before working difficult RTL, verification and hardware-metric scenarios.
Treat FMEDA, fault-injection results and safety-manual claims as one connected, traceable evidence chain rather than standalone numbers.
Make technical-management, certification and customer-integration decisions using explicit assumptions and residual gaps.

caseStudy.title: A Lockstep CPU Core for Multiple Automotive Customers
caseStudy.description: A semiconductor IP vendor develops a dual-core lockstep CPU as a Safety Element out of Context intended for ASIL D braking and steering applications across several OEM and Tier-1 customers, from RTL through tapeout, characterization and multi-customer safety-manual support.

notice: Employer-neutral learning material. Coverage draws on public functional-safety, verification and semiconductor-industry practice. Licensed standards, foundry data and customer-approved safety cases remain authoritative.

architectureExercise.title: 45-minute lockstep IP safety-case exercise
architectureExercise.prompt: Design and defend the end-to-end functional safety approach for a new dual-core lockstep CPU IP core intended for ASIL D automotive use across multiple customers, from element boundary through RTL, verification, hardware metrics and safety-manual support.
structure: Define the element boundary, assumed ASIL and Assumptions of Use.
Select and justify the redundancy architecture (lockstep, delayed lockstep or TMR) against latency/area/power constraints.
Plan separate functional and safety-mechanism verification, including formal properties for the comparator.
Build the FMEDA and fault-injection plan, and derive SPFM/LFM/PMHF with stated assumptions.
Author the safety manual and AoU for multiple customer configurations.
Define the pre-tapeout review gates and the certification-support plan.
challenges: The comparator itself has no independent self-check in the initial design.
Two customers propose conflicting interpretations of the same Assumptions of Use.
A physical-design deadline threatens to compress the pre-tapeout safety review.
An assessor finds the evidence technically complete but scattered across disconnected repositories.

days.title: Semiconductor Functional Safety Foundations
days.focus: Element vs. item development, SEooC, assumed ASIL, and why silicon-level evidence has to be traceable by name.
days.deliverable: Write the element boundary and Assumptions of Use for one silicon safety mechanism.

days.title: Digital Design Fundamentals for Safety Engineers
days.focus: Combinational/sequential logic, clock-domain crossings, synthesis, and DFT's dual role as test and diagnostic infrastructure.
days.deliverable: Review a synchronizer and a DFT/diagnostic overlap for one safety-relevant path.

days.title: The Semiconductor Design and Safety Lifecycle
days.focus: Spec-to-production design flow, tapeout as an irreversible gate, and configuration management under a fixed SOP date.
days.deliverable: Map safety work products and review gates across a design-flow schedule.

days.title: RTL Verification Strategy
days.focus: Simulation, formal verification and emulation; functional coverage versus safety-mechanism verification.
days.deliverable: Design a verification strategy that separately evidences function and fault detection for one mechanism.

days.title: Fault Injection and Silicon-Level Safety Analysis
days.focus: Gate-level fault models, IP-block FMEDA, and fault-injection campaigns that substantiate coverage claims.
days.deliverable: Build a mini FMEDA and fault-injection plan for one safety mechanism.

days.title: Lockstep, Redundancy and Diagnostic Hardware Architectures
days.focus: Lockstep, delayed lockstep, TMR, comparator self-check, and independence under shared clock/power.
days.deliverable: Select and justify a redundancy architecture against a stated latency/area/power constraint.

days.title: Hardware Safety Metrics for IP and SoC
days.focus: SPFM/LFM/PMHF from the producer's side, base failure rate sourcing, and sensitivity analysis.
days.deliverable: Produce a metric sensitivity table across a test-interval assumption range.

days.title: Safety Element out of Context: the Producer's Side
days.focus: Authoring Assumptions of Use and a safety manual from the producer's side, and the assumed-ASIL business risk.
days.deliverable: Draft AoU entries and a safety-manual outline for a multi-customer IP block.

days.title: Standards Landscape: IEC 61508, ISO/SAE 21434 and ASPICE
days.focus: ISO 26262's IEC 61508 lineage, ISO/SAE 21434 TARA versus HARA, and ASPICE HWE process capability.
days.deliverable: Analyze a safety/security seam (e.g. secure boot) and its joint review requirement.

days.title: Certification, Assessment and Technical Leadership
days.focus: Assessment types, safety-case packaging, multi-audience defense, and end-to-end technical leadership.
days.deliverable: Present a 15-minute safety-case argument and end-to-end approach for a new lockstep IP core.

quiz.q: A supplier calls their IP core “ASIL D ready.” What single piece of missing evidence should make you most skeptical of the claim?
options: A marketing brochure describing the core's performance
A safety manual and Assumptions of Use that trace the claim to a defined FMEDA and metrics
A press release announcing automotive design wins
A roadmap slide showing future process-node support
quiz.why: An ASIL claim is only as credible as the traceable safety plan, FMEDA, metrics and Assumptions of Use behind it; without that chain it is an assertion, not evidence.

quiz.q: A safety mechanism shows 100% code coverage in RTL simulation. What does this actually confirm?
options: That the safety mechanism correctly detects and reacts to every fault it claims to cover
That every line or branch of the mechanism's RTL executed during testing, independent of whether its fault-detecting behavior was exercised
That the mechanism is synthesis-clean and timing-closed
That the mechanism's diagnostic coverage meets its SPFM/LFM target
quiz.why: Code coverage measures execution, not correctness under fault conditions; a mechanism can be fully exercised functionally while its fault-detecting path is never actually triggered by any test.

quiz.q: Two lockstep cores share a single clock tree and power rail. What can be claimed about their independence without further analysis?
options: Full independence, since lockstep itself guarantees redundancy
Independence from each core's own internal logic faults, but not from a shared clock-glitch or supply-droop event
No independence at all under any circumstance
Independence is irrelevant once a comparator is present
quiz.why: Shared clock and power are common-cause failure sources that lockstep alone does not address; a dependent-failure analysis or mitigation such as delayed lockstep is needed before that specific independence claim is credible.
